The Model 1861 had a general effective range of 200 to 400 yards (180–370 m) but could reliably hit man-sized targets out to 500 yards (460 m) when used by marksmen, and used percussion caps which were much more reliable and weather resistant to fire (rather than the flintlocks of the 18th century; the last U.
Well-trained troops were able to fire at a rate of three aimed shots per minute while maintaining accuracy up to 500 yards (460 m), though firing distances in the war were often much shorter.

The most notable difference between the Model 1861 and the earlier Springfield Model 1855 was the elimination of the Maynard tape primer for the Model 1861 (the Maynard primer, a self-feeding primer system, was unreliable in damp conditions, and the priming mechanism was expensive and time-consuming to produce).
Further, unlike the Model 1855, the Model 1861 was never produced in a two-banded rifle configuration.
The sight had two leaves, one for 300 yards (270 m) and the other for 500 yards (460 m), and with both leaves down, the sight was set for a range of 100 yards (91 m).

By contrast, the British Enfield Pattern 1853, favored by the Confederate military, utilized a ladder-sight system with 100-yard (91 m) increments, using steps from 100 to 400 yards (91–366 m) and a flip-up ladder for ranges beyond 500 yards (460 m).

The Enfield's sights also extended to 900 yards (820 m) (and further, on later models), compared to the 500-yard (460 m) maximum range of the Model 1861's sights, but for the average infantryman hitting anything beyond 600 yards (550 m) with either weapon was mostly a matter of luck.
The most notable producer of contract Model 1861 rifled muskets was Colt, who made several minor design changes in their version, the "Colt Special" rifled musket.

== History == The Model 1861 was relatively scarce in the early years of the Civil War (many troops were still using Springfield Model 1842 smoothbore muskets and Springfield Model 1816 flintlock muskets converted to percussion cap primers due to better reliability and weather resistance, both in .
69 caliber).
However, over time, more and more regiments began receiving Model 1861 rifled muskets, though this upgrade appeared somewhat quicker in the Eastern Theater of Operations.

Lorenz rifle.title: Lorenz rifle
sentences: The Lorenz rifle saw combat during the Second Italian War of Independence in 1859 and the Austro-Prussian War in 1866.

== History ==   === Austria === The Lorenz rifle was designed by Austrian lieutenant Joseph Lorenz and adopted by the Imperial Austrian Army in 1854, replacing the Augustin musket in 1855, though by late 1859 not all army regiments received the Lorenz due to slow deliveries, while most of the soldiers who did received them weren't properly trained to fully take advantage of the Lorenz long range accuracy.

Despite suffering a large number of casualties during the Second Schleswig War due to their reliance on the Stoßtaktik and witnessing the firepower of the Dreyse needle gun, the Austrians would not begin to replace the Lorenz with breechloader rifles until the end of the Austro-Prussian War, partly for economical reasons: the Vienna arsenal managed to ramp up production to 1,000 rifles per day in 1862 by adopting new machinery and introducing a breechloader design would require a costly retooling of government factories.

During the Austro-Prussian War, the Austrian infantry a mix of Model 1854 and the Model 1862 Lorenz rifles; while it was slower to reload than the Dreyse needle gun, it had a superior range over the Prussian rifle, though reliance on the Stoßtaktik—which proved effective against the Italians as they lacked quick-firing breechloaders—effectively negated this advantage; After sustaining heavy losses during the initial battles against the Prussians, the Austrian Commander Ludwig von Benedek ordered a return to fire tactics to counter Prussian firepower, but his subordinates continued to launch assault columns at the enemy lines, contributing to the Austrian defeat in the Battle of Königgrätz.

After the war, Archduke Albrecht demanded the Austrian infantry to be re-equipped immediately in August 1866 and in response, the Lorenz was hastily converted into a breechloader design, the Wänzl rifle as an emergency measure; In the following year, the Werndl–Holub rifle—which was previously rejected by the Austrian military—was formally adopted.
In the late 19th century surplus Lorenz rifles were sold in Africa as trade guns.

The Tyler Ordnance Works in Texas produced hundreds of Lorenz copies for the Confederate Army between 1863 and 1865, while the Confederate arsenal in Raleigh was responsible for manufacturing the corresponding ammunition using molds imported by blockade runners.

In the early 1860s, the Austrian artillery officer General Wilhelm Lenk von Wolfsberg experimented with guncotton to create an experimental smokeless powder cartridge for the Model 1854 Lorenz; some of these cartridges were carried—but not used in actual combat—during the Second Schleswig War to test for any signs of deterioration; while the results were deemed as promising, with Von Lenk's cartridges remaining undamaged after being carried by troops for months and shooting just as well as new cartridges, Von Lenk's experiments were ultimately abandoned following multiple cases of explosions in 1862 and 1865 that were traced back to spontaneous combustion caused by the deterioration of impurities left by the guncotton manufacturing process at the time.
